subject: Environment
description: Covers Water Act, Air Act, EPA 1986, NGT jurisdiction, EPR, and NAQI.

questions.stem: The Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB), the apex anti-pollution body in India, was constituted under which environmental legislation?

options.option_text: The Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974
The Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1981
The Environment (Protection) Act, 1986
The National Green Tribunal Act, 2010

questions.explanation:
WHY IT IS CORRECT: The Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) is a statutory organization. It was established in September 1974 strictly under the Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974. Later, when the Air Act was passed in 1981, the powers and functions to control air pollution were simply entrusted to this already existing board, rather than creating a new one.
DECOY BUSTING: It is a common misconception that the CPCB was formed under the broad Environment (Protection) Act of 1986. The EPA 1986 acts as an umbrella act, but the CPCB predates it by 12 years. 
EXAM INSIGHT: State Pollution Control Boards (SPCBs) were also created under the same Water Act of 1974. They enforce both Water and Air Acts at the state level. The CPCB advises the Central Government, sets national air and water quality standards, and coordinates the activities of SPCBs.

questions.stem: Which environmental legislation in India was enacted urgently in the direct aftermath of the Bhopal Gas Tragedy?

options.option_text: The Environment (Protection) Act, 1986
The Public Liability Insurance Act, 1991
The Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1981
The Hazardous Wastes Management Rules, 1989

questions.explanation:
WHY IT IS CORRECT: The Environment (Protection) Act (EPA) of 1986 was enacted under Article 253 of the Constitution (which empowers the Union to enact laws implementing international agreements, specifically the 1972 Stockholm Declaration). However, the immediate domestic trigger was the catastrophic Bhopal Gas Tragedy in December 1984. The tragedy exposed glaring loopholes in India's fragmented environmental laws (the Water and Air acts were insufficient to handle industrial chemical disasters).
DECOY BUSTING: The Public Liability Insurance Act 1991 was also a result of Bhopal (to provide immediate relief to victims of hazardous substance accidents), but the EPA was the primary, immediate legislative overhaul. The Air Act predates Bhopal.
EXAM INSIGHT: The EPA 1986 is considered an "umbrella legislation." It gives the Central Government immense, sweeping powers to close down industries, issue directions, lay down emission standards, and declare ecologically sensitive zones. It remains the most powerful environmental law in India.

questions.stem: Under the Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1981, noise pollution was initially not covered. In which year was the Act amended to legally classify noise as an air pollutant?
questions.explanation:
WHY IT IS CORRECT: When the Air Act was enacted in 1981, it focused entirely on traditional atmospheric pollutants (smoke, gases, particulate matter). Recognizing the severe health impacts of noise in industrial and urban settings, the government amended the Air Act in 1987. The amendment legally redefined "air pollutant" to explicitly include "noise."
DECOY BUSTING: The Noise Pollution (Regulation and Control) Rules were formulated much later in 2000 under the Environment Protection Act, which set ambient noise standards for different zones (industrial, commercial, residential, silence). But the legal recognition of noise as an air pollutant occurred in 1987.
EXAM INSIGHT: This legal quirk means that State Pollution Control Boards can use the draconian powers of the Air Act to shut down factories or seize equipment solely for excessive noise, without needing a separate noise legislation. Questions regarding the 1987 amendment are frequent in State PSCs and SSC.

questions.stem: The National Green Tribunal (NGT), established in 2010, operates on the principle of natural justice rather than being bound by the Code of Civil Procedure. Which of the following acts is outside the jurisdiction of the NGT?

options.option_text: The Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972
The Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974
The Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980
The Environment (Protection) Act, 1986

questions.explanation:
WHY IT IS CORRECT: The National Green Tribunal Act, 2010 grants the NGT jurisdiction over civil cases involving substantial questions relating to the environment arising out of SEVEN specific laws. Crucially, two major environmental laws are EXCLUDED from NGT's jurisdiction: The Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972, and the Indian Forest Act, 1927. Cases involving poaching or tiger reserves must go to regular criminal/civil courts.
DECOY BUSTING: The seven laws the NGT CAN enforce are: The Water Act (1974), Water Cess Act (1977), Forest Conservation Act (1980), Air Act (1981), Environment Protection Act (1986), Public Liability Insurance Act (1991), and Biological Diversity Act (2002).
EXAM INSIGHT: This limitation is a favorite trick question in UPSC Prelims. NGT deals heavily with pollution and forest clearance (under FCA 1980), but cannot hear cases about wildlife crime or rights of tribals under the Forest Rights Act 2006.

questions.stem: What is the primary objective of the 'Extended Producer Responsibility' (EPR) framework embedded in India's E-Waste and Plastic Waste Management Rules?

options.option_text: Making the manufacturer physically and financially responsible for the environmentally sound management of their products at the end of their useful life
Mandating that manufacturers must provide a minimum 5-year warranty on all consumer electronics
Shifting the entire cost of municipal waste collection from local governments to the consumers
Requiring industries to plant trees equivalent to the carbon footprint of their manufacturing process

questions.explanation:
WHY IT IS CORRECT: Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) is an environmental policy approach. Traditionally, once a company sold a TV or a plastic bottle, what happened to it afterward was the consumer's and municipality's problem. EPR legally forces the brand owner/manufacturer to take responsibility for the "end-of-life" stage of the product. They must set up collection centres and ensure safe recycling or disposal.
DECOY BUSTING: It is about waste management, not consumer warranties, carbon offsetting, or taxing citizens. It shifts the burden from the municipality to the producer.
EXAM INSIGHT: EPR is the cornerstone of the E-Waste (Management) Rules, 2016, and the Plastic Waste Management Rules, 2016. If a smartphone company sells 1 million phones in India, they have an EPR target to collect and recycle a certain percentage of that weight in e-waste. Non-compliance results in heavy environmental compensation fines.

questions.stem: Under the Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974, what is the meaning of 'Consent to Establish' (CTE) and 'Consent to Operate' (CTO)?

options.option_text: Mandatory permissions industries must obtain from the State Pollution Control Board before building a plant, and again before starting operations
Certificates issued by the Central Ground Water Authority to extract groundwater for agriculture
Agreements signed between two states to share river water without pollution disputes
Taxes paid by polluting industries to fund municipal water treatment plants

questions.explanation:
WHY IT IS CORRECT: CTE and CTO are the foundational regulatory tools of the Water and Air Acts. Any industry or process that is likely to discharge sewage or trade effluent into a stream, well, or sewer must apply to the State Pollution Control Board (SPCB). 
- Consent to Establish (CTE): Required BEFORE construction begins. 
- Consent to Operate (CTO): Required after construction, BEFORE actual production/discharge starts, verifying that promised pollution control equipment (like Effluent Treatment Plants) is installed.
DECOY BUSTING: They are regulatory licenses, not water sharing treaties, groundwater extraction permits, or taxes.
EXAM INSIGHT: Operating without these consents is a criminal offense. The SPCB can immediately cut off electricity and water supply to any industry found operating without a valid CTO. This dual-consent mechanism is India's primary defense against industrial pollution.

questions.stem: Which index was launched by the Ministry of Environment, Forests and Climate Change to disseminate information on air quality in an easily understandable format to the general public?

options.option_text: National Air Quality Index (NAQI)
Comprehensive Environmental Pollution Index (CEPI)
System of Air Quality and Weather Forecasting And Research (SAFAR)
Air Pollution Action Plan Index

questions.explanation:
WHY IT IS CORRECT: The National Air Quality Index (NAQI) was launched in 2014 under the Swachh Bharat Abhiyan. Its core philosophy is "One Number- One Colour-One Description" to simplify complex air quality data. It categorizes air quality into six categories (Good, Satisfactory, Moderately polluted, Poor, Very Poor, and Severe) using color codes. It considers 8 pollutants (PM10, PM2.5, NO2, SO2, CO, O3, NH3, and Pb).
DECOY BUSTING: CEPI is used by CPCB to identify critically polluted industrial clusters (like Vapi or Ankleshwar), not for daily public information. SAFAR is an advanced research and forecasting system developed by the Indian Institute of Tropical Meteorology (IITM), Pune, which feeds data into the AQI, but is not the index itself.
EXAM INSIGHT: In Delhi-NCR, when the NAQI hits the 'Severe' category, emergency measures under the Graded Response Action Plan (GRAP)—such as banning construction and stopping diesel trucks—are automatically triggered.

questions.stem: Section 2(a) of the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 defines the term 'environment'. Which of the following most accurately reflects that statutory definition?

options.option_text: Water, air, land, and their interrelationship with all living creatures and property
Only water bodies and atmospheric air in their unmodified natural states
Land and forest resources specifically identified by the Central Government
Air, water, and soil within legally notified ecologically sensitive zones

questions.explanation: A is correct because Section 2(a) of EPA 1986 defines 'environment' to include water, air, and land and the inter-relationship which exists among and between them, and human beings, other living creatures, plants, micro-organisms, and property. Option B is wrong because the definition is not limited to water and air — it expressly includes land and all living organisms, making it far broader than just two physical media. Option D is wrong because the definition is not geographically restricted to notified zones.

questions.stem: Under the Noise Pollution (Regulation and Control) Rules, 2000, what is the permissible ambient noise limit (Leq in dB(A)) for a 'Silence Zone' during daytime hours (6 a.m. to 10 p.m.)?

options.option_text: 45 dB(A) — the limit set for residential areas at night time
55 dB(A) — the standard applicable to residential areas by day
50 dB(A) — the prescribed daytime limit for silence zones
65 dB(A) — the ceiling for commercial zones during daytime

questions.explanation: C is correct because Schedule I of the Noise Pollution Rules, 2000 fixes 50 dB(A) as the daytime ambient noise standard for Silence Zones, which include areas within 100 metres of hospitals, educational institutions, and courts. Option A (45 dB(A)) is the Residential zone night-time limit — a classic exam trap because it is close to the correct figure. Option B (55 dB(A)) is the Residential daytime standard, and Option D (65 dB(A)) applies to Commercial zones during daytime.

questions.stem: The Solid Waste Management Rules, 2016 mandate generators to segregate waste at source before handing it over to collectors. Into how many streams must this segregation be carried out?

options.option_text: Two streams: biodegradable waste and non-biodegradable recyclable waste
Four streams: organic, recyclable, inert, and construction debris
Five streams as mandated under the Basel Convention framework norms
Three streams: wet waste, dry waste, and domestic hazardous waste

questions.explanation: D is correct because Rule 4(1) of the SWM Rules, 2016 explicitly requires generators to segregate solid waste into three separate streams: bio-degradable (wet), non-bio-degradable (dry/recyclable), and domestic hazardous waste (sanitary napkins, diapers, expired medicines, etc.). Option A (two streams) reflects the older binary approach of the Municipal Solid Waste Rules, 2000, which the 2016 Rules replaced. Option C is a red herring — the Basel Convention governs transboundary movement of hazardous waste, not domestic source segregation.

questions.stem: The Bio-Medical Waste Management Rules, 2016 prescribe a colour-coded bag system for segregation. Which colour bag is designated for human anatomical waste such as body parts, tissues, and organs?

options.option_text: Yellow bag, designated for anatomical and soiled chemical wastes
Red bag, used for contaminated recyclable plastic waste items
White translucent bag, used for sharps like needles and scalpels
Blue bag, meant for glassware and metallic body implants

questions.explanation: A is correct because Schedule I of the BMW Management Rules, 2016 assigns Category 1 waste — including human anatomical waste (body parts, tissues, organs) and animal anatomical waste — to Yellow bags/containers for mandatory incineration. Option B (Red bag) is the most tempting distractor; it is for Category 3 contaminated recyclable plastics like IV tubes and catheter bags. White/translucent bags handle Category 6 sharps, and Blue containers hold Category 7 glassware and metallic implants.

questions.stem: The Hazardous and Other Wastes (Management and Transboundary Movement) Rules, 2016 were enacted to replace which immediately preceding set of rules in India?

options.option_text: Hazardous Wastes (Management and Handling) Rules, 1989, as amended in 2003
Hazardous Chemical Substances (Management and Control) Amendment Rules, 2004
Hazardous Wastes (Management, Handling and Transboundary Movement) Rules, 2008
Hazardous and Toxic Waste (Management, Handling and Disposal) Rules, 2009

questions.explanation: C is correct because the 2016 Rules directly superseded the Hazardous Wastes (Management, Handling and Transboundary Movement) Rules, 2008, which were themselves a comprehensive revision of the original 1989 framework. Option A is the most tempting distractor — the 1989 Rules were the founding framework — but the 2016 Rules replaced the immediately preceding 2008 version, not the 1989 text. Options B and D describe rule sets that do not exist in Indian environmental law.

questions.stem: Under Section 15(1) of the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986, if a contravention persists even after the first conviction, what additional financial penalty is prescribed for each day of the continuing violation?

options.option_text: ₹1,000 per day as set in the original 1986 text of Section 15
₹10,000 per day as revised under a 1991 amendment to the EPA
₹25,000 per day indexed to environmental damage assessment norms
₹5,000 per day for each day of the continuing default or violation

questions.explanation: D is correct because Section 15(1) of EPA 1986 prescribes an additional fine which may extend to ₹5,000 for every day during which the failure or contravention continues after the date of first conviction. The base penalty for a first contravention is imprisonment up to 5 years and/or a fine up to ₹1 lakh. Options A, B, and C cite figures (₹1,000; ₹10,000; ₹25,000) that do not appear in Section 15 — they are calibrated to trap candidates who conflate penalty provisions across the Water Act, Air Act, and EPA.

questions.stem: The National Green Tribunal Act, 2010 gives NGT jurisdiction only over disputes arising from statutes listed in Schedule I. Which of the following Acts is NOT included in that Schedule?

options.option_text: The Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972 covering endangered species
The Biological Diversity Act, 2002 covering access and benefit sharing
The Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Cess Act, 1977
The Public Liability Insurance Act, 1991 on industrial accidents

questions.explanation: A is correct because the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972 is conspicuously absent from Schedule I of the NGT Act, 2010. NGT therefore cannot take cognisance of cases arising solely under the Wildlife Act — such disputes go to civil courts or the High Court. Schedule I lists seven statutes: the Water Act 1974, Water Cess Act 1977 (Option C), Forest Conservation Act 1980, Air Act 1981, EPA 1986, Public Liability Insurance Act 1991 (Option D), and Biological Diversity Act 2002 (Option B). Candidates routinely assume that because the Wildlife Act is environment-related, NGT covers it — it does not.
